###### **compare_floorplans**

Writes a report that lists any differences in objects and their locations between the
current design and floorplan information for another design written by the _write_floorplan_
command.

**Syntax**

int _compare_floorplans_
```
[-input dir_name ]
[-verbosity minimum | low | high]
[-top_level_only]
```

**Data Types**
```
dir_name string
```

**Arguments**
```
-input dir_name
```

Specifies the name of the directory under which the file
_floorplan_compare_data.txt_ is located. The default is _./floorplan_ . The command
writes an error message and exits if the directory does not exist, or if the file is
missing.




```
-verbosity minimum | low | high
```

Determines the level of comparison detail to report. The _minimum_ argument
prints the number of differences for each object type. The _low_ argument prints
up to five examples for each object type. The _high_ argument prints up to 1000
differences of each type. By default, the level is minimum.
```
-top_level_only
```

Compares only top-level objects and skip comparison for lower-level objects.

**Description**

The _compare_floorplans_ command creates a report containing a list of objects that are
either in _floorplan_compare_data.txt_ file but not in the design database, or in the design
database but not in _floorplan_compare_data.txt_ . The object types that are considered
are macros and pins. Feedthrough pins are not considered. The command creates a file
named _compare_output_, in the current directory, that creates lists of new objects that are
in the existing in database but not in the file. For example:
```
set _new_macros [get_cells { macro1_name macro2_name ...}]
set _new_ports {...}
```

For objects in the _floorplan_compare_data.txt_ file but not in the database, the command
outputs names and locations or boundaries in the same file. The command outputs two
levels, for example, pins and macros at the top level and inside blocks. The command
skips the output for the third level and beyond.

Note that the _floorplan_compare_data.txt_ file is generated by the _write_floorplan_
command. The _compare_floorplans_ command is typical used to compare different versions
of the same design. For example, begin by running the _write_floorplan_ command on
one version of the design. Then, load the new version and use the _compare_floorplans_
command to determine if any differences exist between the two versions.

This command returns 1 on success, 0 otherwise.

**Examples**

The following example writes a report based on comparing the current design with the
_floorplan_compare_data.txt_ file in the script directory.
```
prompt> compare_floorplans -input script
```

The following example prints more detailed information, but outputs data related to the toplevel only.
```
prompt> compare_floorplans -verbosity high -top_level_only

```

**See Also**

 - write_floorplan




###### **compare_libraries**

Compare the content and analysis results between two libraries.

**Syntax**

status _compare_libraries_
```
-ref_lib library_object
-target_lib library_object
-ref_lib_analysis analysis_name
-target_lib_analysis analysis_name
[-all | -inv_buf | -combinational | -sequential | -registers | -latch |
-families family_name_string_list | -custom_pairs file_name ]
[-attributes attribute_name_string_list ]
[-lex_attr_mapping file_name ]
[-ref_lib_opcond opcond_name_string | -ref_lib_ppvt ppvt_label_string ]
[-target_lib_opcond opcond_name_string | -target_lib_ppvt
string ppvt_label_string ]
[-slew_point slew_value | -slew_index slew_index \
[-load_point load_value | -load_index load_index \
[-output_comparison_pairs file_name ]
[-verbose]
[-show_absolute_values]
[-significant_digits digits ]
[-plot]
[-plot_title plot_title_string ]
```

**Data Types**
```
library_object        library-object
analysis_name        string
family_name_string_list   list-of-strings
attribute_name_string_list  list-of-strings
file_name          string
opcond_name_string      string
ppvt_label_string      string
slew_value          float
load_value          float
slew_index          integer
load_index          integer
plot_title_string      string
```

**Arguments**
```
-ref_lib library_object
```

The reference library as the comparison baseline.




```
-target_lib library_object
```

The target library to be compared against the reference library. This is allowed
be the same to the reference library for comparing the properties under different
operating conditions.
```
-ref_lib_analysis analysis_name
```

The analysis name which the reference library was analyzed.
```
-target_lib_analysis analysis_name
```

The analysis name which the target library was analyzed.
```
-all
```

Compare all library cells.
```
-inv_buf
```

Compare all inverters and buffers.
```
-combinational
```

Compare all combinational cells.
```
-sequential
```

Compare all sequential cells.
```
-registers
```

Compare all register cells (Flip-Flops).
```
-latch
```

Compare all latch cells.
```
-families family_name_string_list
```

Compare all library cells in the specified library cell families.
```
-custom_pairs file_name
```

Compare the library cell pairs as defined in the file.
```
-lex_attr_mapping file_name
```

The lexical attribute values mapping relationship between the reference and the
target libraries.
```
-attributes attribute_name_string_list
```

The attributes to be compared. The allowed attributes are {area, avg_pin_cap,
avgsl_rise_drive, avgsl_fall_drive, avgsl_rise_delay, avgsl_fall_delay,
avgsl_rise_setup, avgsl_fall_setup, avgsl_rise_hold, avgsl_fall_hold,
avgsl_rise_ckq, avgsl_fall_ckq, avgsl_rise_bht, avgsl_fall_bht, leakage,




internal_power, switch_power, dynamic_power}. If this argument is not provided,
by default all the attributes will be compared and reported.
```
-ref_lib_opcond opcond_name_string
```

The operating condition of the reference library to be compared, specified by
operating condition name. It must be analyzed by _run_library_analysis_ .
```
-target_lib_opcond opcond_name_string
```

The operating condition of the target library to be compared, specified by
operating condition name. It must be analyzed by _run_library_analysis_ .
```
-ref_lib_ppvt ppvt_label_string
```

The operating condition of the reference library to be compared, specified with
the format {Process Label, Process, Voltage, Temperature}. It must be analyzed
by _run_library_analysis_ . If the Process Label is not defined in the library thus it
is empty, use the reserved keyword (none). Examples: {Typical, 1.0, 0.85, 25},
{(none), 1.0, 0.85, 25}
```
-target_lib_ppvt ppvt_label_string
```

The operating condition of the target library to be compared, specified with the
format {Process Label, Process, Voltage, Temperature}. It must be analyzed
by _run_library_analysis_ . If the Process Label is not defined in the library thus it
is empty, use the reserved keyword (none). Examples: {Typical, 1.0, 0.85, 25},
{(none), 1.0, 0.85, 25}
```
-slew_point slew_value
```

The input slew condition of this comparison, specified by the absolute value.
This slew point must be analyzed by _run_library_analysis_ .
```
-slew_index slew_index
```

The input slew condition of this comparison, specified by the index of the slew
points given to _run_library_analysis_ .
```
-load_point load_value
```

The output load condition of this comparison, specified by the absolute value.
This output load must be analyzed by _run_library_analysis_ .
```
-load_index load_index
```

The output load condition of this comparison, specified by the index of the output
load given to _run_library_analysis_ .
```
-output_comparison_pairs file_name
```

To write out a file listing the library cell comparison pairs. This file is written in the
file format taken by the argument _-custom_pairs_ .




```
-verbose
```

Report the results in verbose mode, with more information.
```
-show_absolute_values
```

In verbose mode, report the reference and the target library cells' absolute
values in addition to the change percentage. Verbose mode will be automatically
enabled when this option is specified.
```
-significant_digits digits
```

Specifies the number of digits to the right of the decimal point to report. This
applies to absolute values and does not apply to the change percentage
numbers. The allowed values are from 5 to 13. The default is 5.
```
-plot
```

Create plots on GUI for the comparison results. Use _start_gui_ to initialize GUI
before executing the command with this argument.
```
-plot_title plot_title_string
```

The title of the plots created on GUI.

**Description**

This command allows users to compare the analysis results and contents between two
libraries. In addition, the interested operating conditions can be specified individually to
the reference library and the target library. Users can also compare the same library under
different operating conditions.

Library cells in the reference library and the target library are compared on each attributes.
A report showing the comparison results will be given. Plots can be created on GUI by
specifying _-plot_ . Use _start_gui_ to initialize GUI before executing the command with _-plot_ .

Before executing this command, the user needs to run _run_library_analysis_ to analyze the
libraries. The reference library is the baseline for comparison; the results of target library
is compared against the reference library. A change +/- % will be given for each attribute
of each library cell, 0% means the results in the reference library and the target library are
the same. A +/- X% change means the number in the target library is X% larger/smaller
than the number in the reference library.

This command iterates each library cell from the reference library (reference library cell),
and searches for a matched library cell from the target library (target library cell). These
two library cells forms a matching pair {reference library cell, target library cell}. The
comparisons are later performed on each matching pair.

The matching is based on library cell names. By default, the reference & target library
cells' full names are used as the matching condition. This is useful when two libraries
with same library cell naming are compared. For libraries with very similar but not exactly




matched cell namings, the matching method can be adjusted to use lexical attributes
extracted by lexical classification, instead of using the full cell name.

To use lexical attributes, the reference and target libraries must be lexical classified
by _classify_lib_cell_attributes_ . These lexical attributes _lexical_cell_prefix_name_,
_lexical_drive1_name_, and _lexical_drive2_name_ are required to be matched.

If the expected values of the same lexical attribute are different between the reference
and the target libraries (e.g. HVT vs. HighVt), a mapping file can be provided via
_-lex_attr_mapping_ to guide the tool knowing what values should be considered as
equivalent.

The lexical attribute mapping file format, three fields separated by space:
```
A_Lexical_Attribute Value_in_Ref_Lib Valie_in_Target_Lib
E.g.
lexical_cell_prefix_name      ND2 nand2
lexical_device_threshold_voltage  HVT HighVt
lexical_device_threshold_voltage  LVT LowVt
```

Each line defines a mapping relationship. For the above example, when the tool checks
for the lexical attributes _lexical_cell_prefix_name_ of a reference and a target library cell,
the value nand2 seen in the target library cell will be considered as equivalent to the value
ND2 seen in the reference library cell. Same to the defined mapping relationships on
_lexical_device_threshold_voltage_, the tools will consider HVT = HighVt, LVT = LowVt,
between the reference and the target library cells.

The users may manually define the interested library cell comparison pairs with
_-custom_pairs_ . The tool will directly compare those user-defined pairs instead of
automatically searching for the matching pairs.

The file format for library cell pair definitions, two fields separated by space, library names
are not required:
```
A_Cell_in_Ref_Lib  A_Cell_in_Target_Lib
E.g.
INVD1  inv_x1
ND2D4  nand2_x4
DFFD1  dff_x1
```

These app options are available for controlling the matching method to be used for
constructing matching pairs.
```
Matching by full library cell name:
libra.complib.match_full_cell_name (Default: True)
Matching by lexical attributes, the above
libra.complib.match_full_cell_name needs to be set to False.

```



```
True means the attribute needs to be matched.
If a lexical attribute is allowed to be different, set the
corresponded app-option to false.
libra.complib.match_lexical_cell_height
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_cell_tile_width
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_clockgate
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_device_sizing_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_eco
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_layout_density_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_layout_variant_1
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_layout_variant_2
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_multibit
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_circuit_topology_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_device_channel_length
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_device_threshold_voltage
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_device_type
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_delay_opt_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_hold_opt_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_property_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_setup_opt_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_slew_opt_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_symmetry_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_electrical_timing_arc_variant
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_well_substrate_bias_architecture
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_userdef_property_1
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_userdef_property_2
(Default: True)
libra.complib.match_lexical_userdef_property_3
(Default: True)

```



Matching method configuration example 1. The library cell names are exactly matched.
```
Library cells in the reference library Lib1:
INVD1 INVD2 NAND2D1 NAND2D2 FFD1 FFD4
Library cells in the target library Lib2:
INVD1 INVD2 NAND2D1 NAND2D2 FFD1 FFD4
The constructed matching pairs, no additional app-option setting is
required.
{Lib1/INVD1  Lib2/INVD1}
{Lib1/INVD2  Lib2/INVD2}
{Lib1/NAND2D1 Lib2/NAND2D1}
{Lib1/NAND2D2 Lib2/NAND2D2}
{Lib1/FFD1  Lib2/FFD1}
{Lib1/FFD4  Lib2/FFD4}
```

Matching method configuration example 2. The library cell names are very similar, but not
exactly the same.
```
Library cells in the reference library Lib1:
INVD1 INVD2 NAND2D1 NAND2D2 FFD1 FFD4
Library cells in the target library Lib2:
INVD1HVT INVD2HVT NAND2D1HVT NAND2D2HVT FFD1HVT FFD4HVT
The lexical classification must be successfully executed on both
libraries.
Lib1/INVD1:
lexical_cell_prefix_name  = INV
lexical_drive1_name    = D1
Lib2/INVD1HVT:
lexical_cell_prefix_name     = INV
lexical_drive1_name        = D1
lexical_device_threshold_voltage = HVT
The matching method can be configured in this way to construct proper
matching pairs.
  set_app_options -name libra.complib.match_full_cell_name -value false
-as_user_default

```



```
  set_app_options -name
libra.complib.match_lexical_device_threshold_voltage -value false
-as_user_default
{Lib1/INVD1  Lib2/INVD1HVT}
{Lib1/INVD2  Lib2/INVD2HVT}
{Lib1/NAND2D1 Lib2/NAND2D1HVT}
{Lib1/NAND2D2 Lib2/NAND2D2HVT}
{Lib1/FFD1  Lib2/FFD1HVT}
{Lib1/FFD4  Lib2/FFD4HVT}
```

Matching method configuration example 3. The library cells have same lexical attributes,
but with different values.
```
Library cells in the reference library Lib1:
HVT_INVD1 HVT_INVD2 HVT_NAND2D1 HVT_NAND2D2 HVT_FFD1 HVT_FFD4
Library cells in the target library Lib2:
inv_x1_hvt inv_x2_hvt nd2_x1_hvt nd2_x2_hvt reg_x1_hvt reg_x4_hvt
The lexical classification must be successfully executed on both
libraries.
Lib1/HVT_NAND2D1:
lexical_cell_prefix_name     = NAND2
lexical_drive1_name        = D1
lexical_device_threshold_voltage = HVT
Lib2/nd2_x1_hvt:
lexical_cell_prefix_name     = nd2
lexical_drive1_name        = x1
lexical_device_threshold_voltage = hvt
A lexical attribute mapping file is needed.
lexical_cell_prefix_name     INV   inv
lexical_cell_prefix_name     NAND2  nd2
lexical_cell_prefix_name     FF   reg
lexical_drive1_name        D1   x1
lexical_drive1_name        D2   x2
lexical_drive1_name        D4   x4
lexical_device_threshold_voltage HVT   hvt
The matching method can be configured in this way to construct proper
matching pairs.
  set_app_options -name libra.complib.match_full_cell_name -value false
-as_user_default

```



```
{Lib1/HVT_INVD1  Lib2/inv_x1_hvt}
{Lib1/HVT_INVD2  Lib2/inv_x2_hvt}
{Lib1/HVT_NAND2D1 Lib2/nd2_x1_hvt}
{Lib1/HVT_NAND2D2 Lib2/nd2_x2_hvt}
{Lib1/HVT_FFD1  Lib2/reg_x1_hvt}
{Lib1/HVT_FFD4  Lib2/reg_x4_hvt}
```

This command iterates each matching pair and compare the interested attributes given by
_-attributes_ . The supported attributes are:
```
area       : Cell area
avgsl_rise_drive : Averaged drive (rise)
avgsl_fall_drive : Averaged drive (fall)
avgsl_rise_delay : Averaged delay (rise)
avgsl_fall_delay : Averaged delay (fall)
avgsl_rise_setup : Averaged setup time (rise)
avgsl_fall_setup : Averaged setup time (fall)
avgsl_rise_hold : Averaged hold time (rise)
avgsl_fall_hold : Averaged hold time (fall)
avgsl_rise_ckq  : Averaged clock-to-q delay (rise)
avgsl_fall_ckq  : Averaged clock-to-q delay (fall)
avgsl_rise_bht  : Averaged black hole time (setup time + clock-to-q
delay, rise)
avgsl_fall_bht  : Averaged black hole time (setup time + clock-to-q
delay, fall)
avg_pin_cap   : Averaged input pin capacitance
leakage     : Leakage power
internal_power  : Internal power
switch_power   : Switching power
dynamic_power  : Dynamic power (internal power + switching power)
By default, all the attributes are compared and reported, if -attributes
is not specified.
Note that the timing attributes are named with prefix avgsl, to better
indicate the number is calculated
based on the specified (or the default) input slew and output load.
```

The operating conditions can be specified by an operating condition name or a PPVT
label {Process Label, Process, Voltage, Temperature}, using arguments _-ref_lib_opcond_,
_-target_lib_opcond_, _-ref_lib_ppvt_, or _-target_lib_ppvt_ .

The specified conditions must be covered by the analysis performed on the libraries.
If an operating condition is not specified, the default operating condition used in the
corresponded analysis will be used for comparison.

Different operating conditions can be given to the reference and target libraries, for
comparing the libraries under different operating conditions.




The operating conditions of a library can be reported by _report_lib_ . Use
_report_environments_ to check which operating conditions are set to the analysis
environment used in the corresponded analysis.
```
To specify this operating condition:
Name         Process  Label        Temp   Voltage
-----------------------------------------------------------------------TYPICAL0P85V25C   1.00   typical0p85v25c   25.00   0.85
Use:
  -ref_lib_opcond TYPICAL0P85V25C
  -target_lib_opcond TYPICAL0P85V25C

or
  -ref_lib_ppvt {typical0p85v25c, 1, 0.85, 25}
  -target_lib_ppvt {typical0p85v25c, 1, 0.85, 25}

If the process label is empty, use the keyword (none) to represent an
empty process label.
For example, {(none), 1, 0.85, 25}
```

The interested input slew and output load can be specified using arguments _-slew_point_,
_-slew_index_, _-load_point_, or _-load_index_ .

By default, if input slew or output load is not specified, the first input slew or output load
used in the corresponded analysis will be used for comparison.

The input slew and output load setting of the analysis environment can be reported by
_report_environments_ .
```
To specify the input slew = 0,1, and output load = 0.05:
Name    Libset    OPCond       Slew Points   Load
Points
-----------------------------------------------------------------------env1    libsetA   TYPICAL0P85V25C  0.1, 0.2    0.01, 0.05
Use:
  -slew_point 0.1
  -load_point 0.05

or
  -slew_index 0
  -load_index 1

```



The verbose mode can be activated by specifying _-verbose_ . Under this mode, more
information will be reported, for example:
```
1. Each timing arc of each library cell matching pair, with the absolute
values and the change %.
2. Each library cell matching pair's comparison results.
```

Plots can be created on GUI, by specifying _-plot_ . A plot title can be given by _-plot_title_ . A
live GUI session is a must for plots creation. Use _start_gui_ to initialize a GUi session if it
has not been initialized yet.

Some usage examples:
```
## Use the default operating condition, input slew, and output load
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1 -target_lib_analysis alys2
## Compare same library, under different operating conditions
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib1] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1_TT0P8525C -target_lib_analysis
alys1_FF0P95125C \\
-ref_lib_ppvt {TT, 1.0, 0.85, 25} -target_lib_ppvt {FF,
1.0, 0.95, 125}
## Compare different libraries, under different operating conditions and
a given slew & load condition
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1_TT0P8525C -target_lib_analysis
alys2_FF0P95125C \\
-ref_lib_ppvt {TT, 1.0, 0.85, 25} -target_lib_ppvt {FF,
1.0, 0.95, 125} \\
-slew_point 0.1 -load_point 0.05
## Compare sequential cells only, on a few interested attributes
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1 -target_lib_analysis alys2 \\
-sequential \\
-attributes {avgsl_rise_ckq avgsl_fall_ckq}
## Compare library cells of library cell families defined for the
reference library
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1 -target_lib_analysis alys2 \\
-families {Lib1_initial_INV Lib1_initial_NAND2
Lib1_initial_FF}
## Compare custom-defined comparison pairs
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1 -target_lib_analysis alys2 \\
-custom_pairs user_def_pairs.txt
## Use the default operating condition, input slew, and output load, but
need lexical attribute mapping

```



```
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1 -target_lib_analysis alys2 \\
-lex_attr_mapping lex_attr_mapping.txt
## Report in verbose mode and create plots with a given title
compare_libraries -ref_lib [get_lib Lib1] -target_lib [get_lib Lib2] \\
-ref_lib_analysis alys1 -target_lib_analysis alys2 \\
-verbose \\
-plot -plot_title "Title_1"

```

**See Also**

 - create_environment

 - report_environments

 - run_library_analysis

 - classify_lib_cell_attributes

###### **compare_qor_data**

Generates the QoRsum web application and report for viewing or comparing QoR results.

**Syntax**

status _compare_qor_data_
```
-run_locations run_location_list
[-run_names run_name_list ]
[-output output_dir ]
[-force]
```

**Data Types**
```
run_location_list   list
run_name_list     list
output_dir       string
```

**Arguments**
```
-run_locations run_location_list
```

Specifies a Tcl list of file system paths to the QoR data written by the
_write_qor_data_ command. These paths can be one of the following:

   - The _-output_ directory written by the _write_qor_data_ command

   - The root directory of a Fusion Platform Methodology (FPM) run

   - The _-work_dir_ option of an _explore_design_ run in the RTL Architect tool




If this option is not specified, the _compare_qor_data_ uses ./qor_data as the
run location. The command generates a QoRsum report for only this run, and
assumes that the default _write_qor_data -output_ directory was used.

When using the Fusion Platform Methodology (FPM) flow, the QoR data for
each stage is stored in many different subdirectories. There are two ways
you can combine all of that data into a single run from the perspective of the
QoRsum report.

The first method uses the design or build directory of the FPM run. The build
directory is the root directory of the run that includes the ./scripts_global, results
for the steps, tasks, and QoR data labels/stages in the entire FPM run.

The second method uses one of the step directories from the FPM run. These
directories are the directories immediately below the design or build directory
with names, such as 310_fc_syndp or 320_fc_synpnr. One of these directories
only collects the QoR data for the tasks and QoR data labels/stages of that
particular step.

When using the _explore_design_ command in the RTL Architect tool, many
different runs are generated in subdirectories under the _explore_design_
_-work_dir_ directory. Each of those runs use the _write_qor_data_ command to
capture QoR results.

Use the same work directory used by the _explore_design_ and
_report_explore_design_result_ commands to gather the results from all runs
contained within. You could also use the ./qor_data directory for each of these
runs individually. By default, the work directory for an _explore_design_ run is
named ./work_dir/run_explore_design/design_name.
```
-run_names run_name_list
```

Specifies a Tcl list of one or more names corresponding to the run data in
the _-run_locations_ list. The length of this list must match the length of the
_-run_locations_ list. Use this option to assign descriptive names for each run in
the QoRsum report. By default, runs are assigned names such as Run1, Run2,
Run3 and so on.

You can also use the _set_qor_data_options -run_name_ option during the original
run to give the QoR data a name. The name is used by the _compare_qor_data_
command when creating the QoRsum report. If the _set_qor_data_options_
_-run_name_ and _compare_qor_data -run_names_ commands are both used, the
latter name takes precedence.

Run names have strict naming restrictions to support various file system and
URL naming rules. The allowed characters are numbers (0-9), lowercase letters
(a-z), uppercase letters (A-Z), dash (-), underscore (_), period (.), and plus (+).




```
-output output_dir
```

Specifies the output directory where the QoRsum web-based report is written.
By default, the QoRsum web-based report is written to the ./compare_qor_data
directory.
```
-force
```

Deletes the _-output_ directory so the report can be recreated. By default, the
QoRsum report is not written out if the _-output_ directory already exists.

**Description**

The _compare_qor_data_ command is used to generate the QoRsum web-based report.
This report provides an easy-to-use interface for viewing the QoR results of a single
run through Synopsys tools, or compare the results of multiple runs. Before using the
_compare_qor_data_ command, the QoR data must be captured at one or more stages of
one or more runs of Synopsys tools using the _write_qor_data_ command.

After a run through the full IC Compiler II or Fusion Compiler flow, use the _write_qor_data_
command to capture the QoR data after significant flow stages, such as _compile_fusion_,
_place_opt_, _clock_opt_, _routing_, and _route_opt_ .

Use the _compare_qor_data_ command at any time to provide a summary report of the
progress of a single run or a comparison report of multiple runs. The runs do not have
to be complete to use the _compare_qor_data_ command. One label or stage must be
captured for one run by using the _write_qor_data_ command, so the _compare_qor_data_
command can compile those results into the QoRsum web-based report.

You can view the QoRsum comparison report by using the _view_qor_data_ command.
This command initiates a localhost web server to serve the QoR data on disk to the
web-based report. You can also view the report directly in a supported web browser. For
example, open the index.html file in the output directory to view the report in Firefox. Some
web browser versions have security restrictions that prevent the display of the QoRsum
report data that uses the _file_ protocol. The _view_qor_data_ command provides a more
predictable way to view the data through the _http_ protocol with the localhost server. See
the _view_qor_data_ man page for more details.

**Examples**

The following example uses the _compare_qor_data_ command to point to the results of a
single run in the ./qor_data directory for viewing:
```
prompt> compare_qor_data -run_locations ./qor_data
```

The following example uses a different output directory and forces overwrite of any
previous QoRsum report at that location:
```
prompt> compare_qor_data -run_locations ./qor_data \\
-output ./qor_summary_report -force

```



The following example points to multiple FPM run results for comparison, and gives them
meaningful names:
```
prompt> compare_qor_data -run_locations \\
"/path/to/fpm_run1 /path/to/fpm_run2 /path/to/fpm_run3" \\
-run_names "baseline_SP2 baseline_SP4 high_effort_timing_SP4"

```

**See Also**

 - write_qor_data

 - view_qor_data

 - set_qor_data_options

 - define_qor_data_panel

 - capture_qor_data

 - set_qor_data_metric_properties

###### **compare_supplies**

compares voltage levels or relative ON-ness between two given supplies.

**Syntax**

status _compare_supplies_
```
supply_list
[-on_status]
[-voltage_level]
```

**Data Types**
```
supply_list    list
on_status     boolean
voltage_level   boolean
```

**Arguments**
```
supply_list
```

Specifies a list of 2 supplies. The first supply specified is treated as the
'reference' supply to which the second supply ('specified' supply) will be
compared to. Supplies can either be supply net names or supply set handles.
```
-on_status
```

If specified, this option will return one of 4 values: "equal" if the reference supply
is equal to the specified supply. "more_on" if the specified supply is more ON as
compared to the reference supply. "less_on" if the specified supply is less ON




as compared to the reference supply. "independent" if the specified supply may
be more or less ON as compared to the reference supply depending on the PST
State.
```
-voltage_level
```

If specified, this option will return one of 4 values: "equal", if both reference
and specified supplies are at the same voltage and no level-shifting is needed.
"higher", if reference supply is lower voltage as compared to the specified
supply. "lower", if the reference supply is higher voltage as compared to the
specified supply. "independent, if the reference supply is higher/lower voltage
as compared to the specified supply depending on the PST State. If the two
supplies specified belong to the same correlated supply group, they will be
compared based on the rules for supplies in the same correlated supply group.

**Description**

This command is used to compare voltage levels or relative always-ON levels of two
given supplies. Options -on_status and -voltage_level can be used separately or in
combination. Supplies list must consist of exactly 2 supplies. If the specified supply has no
states defined, we will treat it as equal to the reference supply and return equal for both
on_status and voltage_level.


**See Also**

 - report_pst

###### **compile_advanced_boundary_cells**

Creates and places boundary cells around target objects in current design.

This command is deprecated and will be obsolete in future release. Please use
_compile_targeted_boundary_cells command_ .

**Syntax**

status _compile_advanced_boundary_cells_
```
[-target_objects { target_objects }]
[-include_touching_placement_blockages]
[-ignore_row_orientation]
[-add_placement_blockage]
[-voltage_area { objects }]
```

**Data Types**
```
target_objects    list
```

**Arguments**
```
-target_objects { target_objects }
```

Specifies the target objects to be around with boundary cells in current design.
Objects including macro, voltage area, voltage area shape, placement blockage,
route blockage and core area can be specified.
```
-include_touching_placement_blockages
```

Specifies that when boundary cells are created and placed, placement
blockages those touch specified target objects should be included. By default,
no touching placement blockages are included.




```
-ignore_row_orientation
```

Specifies that when flipping between top and bottom.
```
-add_placement_blockage
```

Add placement blockage to meet boundary cells rules.
```
-voltage_area { objects }
```

Specifies the voltage areas to insert boundary cells.

**Description**

This command adds boundary cells around the boundaries of target objects, such as
voltage areas, macros, blockages, and the core area, according to the boundary cell rules
set by _set_boundary_cell_rules_ .

**Examples**

The following example creates boundary cells around target placement blockages on both
the left and the right edges of boundaries.
```
prompt> set_boundary_cell_rules -left_boundary_cell myLib/CellLeft \\
-right_boundary_cell myLib/CellRight
prompt> compile_advanced_boundary_cells -target_objects {PB_7 PB_8}

```

###### **compile_fusion**

Runs synthesis, placement, and optimization on the current design.

**Syntax**

_compile_fusion_
```
[-list_only]
[-from startStage ]
[-to endStage ]
[-check_only]
```

**Data Types**
```
startStage  string
endStage   string
```

**Arguments**
```
-list_only
```

Prints the major stages that constitute the default flow for the _compile_fusion_
command.

These stages are: _initial_map_, _logic_opto_, _initial_place_, _initial_drc_, _initial_opto_,
_final_place_, and _final_opto_ .

This option cannot be used with the _-from_ and _-to_ options.
```
-from startStage
```

Specifies the starting stage for the _compile_fusion_ command. Valid values are
any of: _initial_map_, _logic_opto_, _initial_place_, _initial_drc_, _initial_opto_, _final_place_,
and _final_opto_ .

The default behavior of _compile_fusion_ without this option is to run from the first
stage that is _initial_map_ .
```
-to endStage
```

Specifies the ending stage for the _compile_fusion_ command. Valid values are
any of: _initial_map_, _logic_opto_, _initial_place_, _initial_drc_, _initial_opto_, _final_place_,
and _final_opto_ .

The default behavior of _compile_fusion_ without this option is to run to the last
stage that is _final_opto_ .

If both the _-to_ and _-from_ options are specified, then all stages from the
_startStage_ until the _endStage_ are run in sequence. The _startStage_ must be the
same or earlier than the _endStage_, in the order shown for the _-list_only_ option.




If the same stage is given for both _startStage_ and _endStage_, then only that
specific stage is run.
```
-check_only
```

Checks for any discrepancy found in the library and design.

If the _-to_ or _-from_ option is specified, the library and design are checked to be
sufficient only for those stages.

**Description**

This command runs during the initial part of the Fusion Compiler flow, running all of the
major logical optimization, physical optimization, and placement operations from synthesis
until clock tree synthesis. In a full Fusion Compiler flow, this command is followed by
_clock_opt_ for clock tree synthesis and post-clock optimization, placement, legalization,
and global routing. This is followed by _hyper_route_opt_ for full routing and post-route
optimization.

The major steps of the _compile_fusion_ flow are:

 - initial_map: Design mapping and minimum area logic optimization

 - logic_opto: Logic-based delay optimization

 - initial_place: Initial coarse placement of the design

 - initial_drc: Buffer tree building for high fanout nets and logical DRC fixing

 - initial_opto: Physical optimization and incremental placement

 - final_place: Incremental placement for timing and congestion improvement and
placement legalization

 - final_opto: Physical optimization for timing and power recovery and placement
legalization

**Examples**

The following example runs all seven stages of the _compile_fusion_ flow. It starts from logic
synthesis and ends up with an optimized design with legalized placement:
```
prompt> compile_fusion
```

The following example runs only the _initial_opto_ stage. It performs physical optimization
and incremental placement to optimize timing and congestion:
```
prompt> compile_fusion -from initial_opto -to initial_opto
```

The following example runs the last two stages of the _compile_fusion_ flow, _final_place_ and
_final_opto_ . It takes in a placed and optimized design as its input, incrementally improves
the placement, and runs more physical optimization and placement legalization.




```
prompt> compile_fusion -from final_place
```

The following example runs the _compile_fusion_ flow from synthesis through initial physical
optimization.
```
prompt> compile_fusion -to initial_opto

```

**See Also**

 - place_opt

###### **compile_logical**

Runs logical synthesis flow on the design.

**Syntax**

_compile_logical_
```
[-check_only]
[-from startStage ]
[-to endStage ]
```

**Arguments**
```
-check_only
```

Checks any discrepancy found in the library and design.
```
-from startStage
```

Specifies the starting stage for the _compile_logical_ command. Valid values are
any of: _initial_map_, _logic_opto_, and _initial_opto_ .

The default behavior of _compile_logical_ without this option is to run from the first
stage that is _initial_map_ .
```
-to endStage
```

Specifies the ending stage for the _compile_fusion_ command. Valid values are
any of: _initial_map_, _logic_opto_, and _initial_opto_ .

The default behavior of _compile_logical_ without this option is to run to the last
stage that is _initial_opto_ .

If both the _-to_ and _-from_ options are specified, then all stages from the
_startStage_ until the _endStage_ are run in sequence. The _startStage_ must be the
same or earlier than the _endStage_, in the order shown for the _-list_only_ option.
If the same stage is given for both _startStage_ and _endStage_, then only that
specific stage is run.




**Description**

By default, the command maps the generic cells to library cells and performs logic
optimization.

The major steps of the _compile_fusion_ flow are:

 - initial_map: Design mapping and minimum area logic optimization

 - logic_opto: Logic-based delay optimization

 - initial_opto: Logical DRC fixing and incremental delay optimization

**Examples**

The following example runs logical compile flow.
```
prompt> compile_logical
```

The following example runs only the _logic_opto_ stage.
```
prompt> compile_logical -from logic_opto -to logic_opto
```

The following example runs the post-compile DFT insertion flow It takes in a mapped
and optimized design as its input, performs DFT insertion and ends up with an optimized
design:
```
prompt> compile_logical -to logic_opto
prompt> insert_dft
prompt> compile_logical -from initial_opto -to initial_opto

```

**See Also**

 - set_non_physical_mode

###### **compile_pg**

Creates a power and ground network including straps, rings, macro connections, standard
cell connections and via connections based on the specified power ground strategies.

**Syntax**

status _compile_pg_
```
[-strategies strategy_list ]
[-via_rule rule_list ]
[-ignore_drc]
[-ignore_via_drc]
[-show_phantom]
[-undo]
[-tag tag_name ]

```



```
[-create_ml_data ]
[-use_ml_model ]
```

**Data Types**
```
strategy_list  list
rule_list    list
tag_name     string
```

**Arguments**
```
-strategies strategy_list
```

Creates a power network based only on the specified list of strategies. By
default, the tool creates a power ground network using all strategies which have
been defined.
```
-via_rule rule_list
```

Specifies the via rule list between strategies and existing shapes. The
via rule list _rule_list_ contains strategy-level via rules defined by the
_set_pg_strategy_via_rule_ command. If no strategy via rule is specified, the
default via defined in the technology file is created at all intersections between
any two orthogonal shapes on different layers.
```
-ignore_drc
```

Creates the power network while ignoring DRCs for both wires and vias. By
default, all DRCs are considered when creating the power network. This option
is mutually exclusive with the _-ignore_via_drc_ option.
```
-ignore_via_drc
```

Creates the power network while ignoring via DRCs. By default, all DRCs are
considered when creating the power network. When this option is set, DRCs for
wires are checked and fixed, DRCs within each stacked via are checked and
fixed. Only DRCs between stacked vias and neighboring objects are ignored.
This option is mutually exclusive with _-ignore_drc_ option.
```
-show_phantom
```

Generates report for wires/vias that should be created but failed due to fixing
DRC violation. Detailed information will be displayed in error browser. The report
includes two parts, phantom wire and phantom via. Wire information and DRC
violation are included in one phantom wire. Only DRC violations that cut part
of wire shape while fixing will be included in phantom wire. Abutted phantom
wires will be merged and reported together. Via information and DRC violation
are included in one phantom via. Via information includes top/bottom wire
information, via def, net name. DRC violation shows initial violation before fixing.
If _-ignore_drc_ or _-ignore_via_drc_ is specified, phantom via will not be generated.




```
-undo
```

Removes the power and ground network created by the most recent _compile_pg_
command.
```
-tag tag_name
```

Specifies a tag name to assign to all new vias and shapes created by this
command. This tag name is used as contents of an user attribute tag for filtering
collections at later stages (see the example in the EXAMPLES section). By
default, no tags are assigned.
```
-create_ml_data
```

This option enables this command to create training data for training ML model
for fixability prediction. When this option is set, the command only creates ML
training data, not creating PG wires/vias.
```
-use_ml_model
```

This option enables this command to load pre-trained ML model for fixability
prediction.

**Description**

This command creates the power network based on the specified power ground
strategies.

Signal routes by default are ignored for DRC checking and correction during PG creation.
Use the following app option to honor signal route DRC during PG creation.
```
prompt> set_app_options -list {plan.pgroute.honor_signal_route_drc true}
```

**Examples**

The following example creates a power ground network using only the example1 and
example2 strategies. The rule1 via rule is defined by the _set_pg_strategy_via_rule_
command.
```
prompt> compile_pg -strategies {example1 example2}\\
-via_rule rule1
```

The following example compiles strategy example1 using 4 threads defined in the global
host_options mt for via creation.
```
prompt> set_host_options -max_cores 4
prompt> compile_pg -strategies {example1}
```

The following example creates collections of vias and wires that are tagged with the name
pg1.




```
prompt> compile_pg -tag pg1
prompt> set vias [get_vias -filter tag==pg1]
prompt> set wires [get_shapes -filter tag==pg1]
```

The following example creates ML training data in memory, output training data to files in
the directory ./pg_model, and train ML model based on the training data. The trained ML
model is stored in the directory ./pg_model.
```
prompt> compile_pg -create_ml_data
prompt> train_pg_ml_model
```

The following example creates ML training data in memory, output training data to files in
directory pg_data_1, and train ML model based on the training data. The trained ML model
is stored in the directory ./pg_model.
```
prompt> compile_pg -create_ml_data
prompt> create_pg_ml_data -output_directory pg_data_1
prompt> train_pg_ml_model -input_directory {pg_data_1}
```

The following example loads pre-trained ML model in the directory ./pg_model for fixability
prediction to reduce runtime of PG via creation.
```
prompt> compile_pg -use_ml_model
```

In addition to the above examples, see the Examples page in the PG Planning section
of the Task Assistant for more information. To view the Examples page, start the GUI
and invoke the following command: _gui_show_task_assistant -task "Design Planning:PG_
_Planning->Examples->Overview"_ .


**See Also**

 - remove_pg_strategies

 - report_pg_strategies

 - report_pg_strategy_via_rules

 - set_host_options

 - set_pg_strategy

 - set_pg_strategy_via_rule

 - get_vias

 - get_shapes

 - create_pg_ml_data

 - train_pg_ml_model




###### **compile_tap_boundary_wall_cells**

Creates and places tap, boundary, and wall cells in current design.

**Syntax**

status _compile_tap_boundary_wall_cells_
```
[-initial_insertion]
[-use_double_height_fill_wall]
[-hdr_n_tap_cells lib_cell_name ]
[-ptap_optimization]
[-second_pass]
```

**Data Types**
```
lib_cell_name      string
```

**Arguments**
```
-initial_insertion
```

Specifies whether inserting only boundary cells and fill-wall cells.
```
-use_double_height_fill_wall
```

Replaces single-height fill-wall with double-height fill-wall.
```
-hdr_n_tap_cells
```

Specifies n-tap type HDR cells. This must be a 2X or 4X row-height cell.
```
-ptap_optimization
```

Specifies whether to replace large PTap cell (2 tall-row height) with small PTap
cell (2 short-row height).
```
-second_pass
```

Enable the process to remove redundant tap cells.

**Description**

This command adds tap, boundary, and wall cells in current block according to the tap,
boundary, and wall cell rules set by the _set_tap_boundary_wall_cell_rules_ command.

**Examples**

The following example creates tap, boundary, and wall cells in current block.
```
prompt> compile_targeted_boundary_cells

###### **compile_targeted_boundary_cells**

Creates and places boundary cells around target objects in current design.

**Syntax**

status _compile_targeted_boundary_cells_
```
[-target_objects target_objects ]
[-include_touching_placement_blockages]
[-ignore_row_orientation]
[-target_boundary polygon ]
[-all_targets]
[-insert_inside_target_boundary]
[-advanced]
```

**Data Types**
```
target_objects    list
polygon collection
```

**Arguments**
```
-target_objects { target_objects }
```

Specifies the target objects to be around with boundary cells in current design.
Objects including macro, voltage area, voltage area shape, placement blockage,
route blockage, and core area can be specified. This is a required option if
all_targets or target_boundary is not set.
```
-include_touching_placement_blockages
```

Specifies that when boundary cells are created and placed, placement
blockages those touch specified target objects should be included. By default,
no touching placement blockages are included.
```
-ignore_row_orientation
```

Specifies that when flipping between top and bottom.




```
-target_boundary
```

Specifies the region to create boundary cells around (outside). This is a required
option if all_targets or target_objects is not set.
```
-all_targets
```

If specified, all voltage areas, placement blockages and macros are used as
targets. This is a required option if target_objects or target_boundary is not set.
```
-insert_inside_target_boundary
```

Used with -target_boundary. Tool inserts boundary cells inside instead of outside
the specified region.
```
-advanced
```

Enable AL-based variable-row engine for boundary cell insertion.

**Description**

This command adds boundary cells around the boundaries of target objects, such as
voltage areas, macros, blockages, and the core area, according to the boundary cell rules
set by _set_boundary_cell_rules_ .

**Examples**

The following example creates boundary cells around target placement blockages on both
the left and the right edges of boundaries.
```
prompt> set_boundary_cell_rules -left_boundary_cell myLib/CellLeft \\
-right_boundary_cell myLib/CellRight
prompt> compile_targeted_boundary_cells -target_objects {PB_7 PB_8}

```

###### **compute_area**

Calculates the area of a geometric region.

**Syntax**

float _compute_area_




```
[-objects object_list ]
[ pos_object_list ]
```

**Data Types**
```
object_list    collection
pos_object_list  collection
```

**Arguments**
```
-objects object_list
```

Specifies the objects to be used to define the geometric region to calculate the
area of. Objects may be a heterogenous collection of poly_rects, geo_masks,
shapes, layers, and other physical objects.

In the case of poly_rects, geo_masks, shapes, or other physical objects, the
resulting area will include the areas of each object. In the case of layers, the
resulting area will include the area of every shape in the layer.

This is a required option if the _pos_object_list_ option is not specified.
```
pos_object_list
```

Specifies the objects to be used to define the geometric region to calculate the
area of. This positional option is provided for compatibility with other tools.

**Description**

This command calculates the area of the region specified by _objects_ .

###### **compute_budget_constraints**

Creates budget pin constraints based on estimate_timing (virtual in-place optimization).




**Syntax**

status _compute_budget_constraints_
```
[-setup_delay]
[-boundary]
[-latency_targets actual | estimated ]
[-busplans buses ]
[-modes mode_list ]
[-estimate_timing]
[-no_estimate_timing]
[-pins pin_list ]
[-input]
[-output]
[-unspecified]
[-feedthrough]
[-slack slack_value ]
[-fanin_cone]
[-fanout_cone]
[-balance true | false ]
[-ocv_percent percent ]
[-ocv_delay delay ]
[-host_options host_options_name ]
[-default]
```

**Data Types**
```
buses     list
mode_list   list
pin_list   list
slack_value  float
percent    float
delay     float
host_options_name  string
```

**Arguments**
```
-setup_delay
```

Calculates budget values for setup delay. See the description section for
more details. You can specify this -setup_delay option in combination with the
_-boundary_ and/or _-latency_targets_ options. If none are specified, setup and
boundaries are computed, that is, the tool behaves the same way as if the user
specified the -setup_delay and -boundary options.
```
-boundary
```

Calculates budget values for drives and loads at the block boundary. See the
description section below for more details. You can specify this -boundary option
in combination with the _-setup_delay_ and/or _-latency_targets_ options. If none
are specified, setup and boundaries are computed, that is, the tool behaves the
same way as if the user specified the -setup_delay and -boundary options.




```
-latency_targets actual | estimated
```

Calculates new clock latency targets to be used during budgeting. You can
specify this -latency_targets option in combination with the _-setup_delay_,
and/or _-boundary_ options. If none are specified, setup and boundaries are
computed, that is, the tool behaves the same way as if the user specified the
-setup_delay and -boundary options. No other budget values are changed.
During budget generation, you can use the clock latency targets to account for
clock tree variation early in the design flow before clock tree synthesis. This
option automatically sets the budget parameters for clock latency targets in your
design. This is equivalent to manually using the _-early_latency_, _-late_latency_
and _-crp_ options with the _set_latency_budget_constraints_ command. You must
specify the _-latency_targets_ option with the _-balance_ option.

The argument to _-latency_targets_ determines how the budget values are
selected. The valid values are:

   - _actual_ : Budget values are selected to closely match the current
clock latencies in your top-level design. The latencies can be either
ideal or propagated, depending on whether your SDC file contains
_set_propagated_clock_ commands.

   - _estimated_ : Budget values are selected to closely match the predicted
latency of your top-level clock tree. The prediction is based on the current
placement of your clock tree elements (the clock trunk, Integrated ClockGating Cells (ICGs), clock pins). The current timing of the clock tree is not
used. Estimated clock latencies are queried from the "clock trunk planning"
tool; therefore, you need to make sure that you have run that first.
```
-busplans buses
```

Automatically determines a fixed budget for segments along a budget
path. This option is equivalent to manually setting the _-delay_ option of the
_set_segment_budget_constraints_ command. Before passing the "buses"
argument, you must first declare them by using the _create_budget_busplan_
command. See the _create_budget_busplan_ command man page for more
details.
```
-modes mode_list
```

Specifies the list of modes to use to create the budget constraints. If this option
is not specified, the command processes all modes with an active corner.
```
-estimate_timing
```

The estimate_timing option is obsoleted and scheduled to be removed in a
subsequent release. Instead, use the plan.budget.estimate_timing_mode
application option.




```
-no_estimate_timing
```

The no_estimate_timing option is obsoleted and scheduled to be removed
in subsequent release. Instead, use the plan.budget.estimate_timing_mode
application option.
```
-pins pin_list
```

Updates budget values for only the specified pins. You can further restrict the list
of pins with the _-input_ and _-output_ options. By default, the command processes
all pins of all budgeted blocks.
```
-input
```

Updates budget values for only input pins to blocks. You can further restrict the
list of pins with the _-pins_ option. By default, the command processes all pins of
all budgeted blocks.
```
-output
```

Updates budget values for only output pins to blocks. You can further restrict the
list of pins with the _-pins_ option. By default, the command processes all pins of
all budgeted blocks.
```
-unspecified
```

Updates budget values for only pins with no existing delay budget. By default,
the command processes all pins of all budgeted blocks.
```
-feedthrough
```

Updates budget values only for paths with feedthroughs. A feedthrough path has
a combinational connection that goes from the input of a block to the output of
a block. By default, the command updates all paths, including those that start or
end in the local block.
```
-slack slack_value
```

Updates budget values only for paths through pins where the budget slack
is less than _slack_value_ . Budget slack is defined as the amount by which the
actual path delay is less than the budgeted path delay. If you specify _-slack 0.0_,
only paths where the budget is tighter than the actual delay are rebudgeted.
```
-fanin_cone
```

Updates budget values only for pins that are in the timing fanin cone of the
selected pins. This is useful when you want to rebudget many pins along the
same path. By default, only selected pins are processed.




```
-fanout_cone
```

Updates budget values only for pins that are in the timing fanout cone of the
selected pins. This is useful when you want to rebudget many pins along the
same path. By default, only selected pins are processed.
```
-balance true | false
```

Sets latency targets as if there is zero skew between two blocks, even if the
current timing analysis shows otherwise. You should set _-balance_ to true
whenever some of your clock timing is propagated (not ideal) or estimated, but
you have not finished balancing your clocks across the whole chip.

During budgeting, it is possible that the clocks of your designs are not yet
balanced. For example, you might have run clock tree synthesis in one of your
blocks and not another. Or, you have run clock tree synthesis in each of your
blocks, but have not yet balanced the blocks with each other. When you set
_-balance_ to true, the budgeter assumes that clocks are balanced.

If you want some clocks in your design to have a latency that is offset from other
clocks, use the _-latency_offset_ option of the _set_latency_budget_constraints_
command to adjust the interclock balance.

You must specify the _-balance_ option together with the _-latency_targets_ option.
```
-ocv_percent percent
```

Adjusts the calculated early and late budget latencies so that they both vary by
at least the specified _percent_ value from the average.

When you use the _-latency_targets_ option, it is possible that on-chip variation
(OCV) is not considered. This happens if you are using ideal clocks and you did
not supply separate early and late latencies. For example, if both the early and
late latency in the design are 10, and you specify _-ocv_percent 5_, the early and
late budget latency targets are set to 9.5 and 10.5, respectively.

You must specify the _-ocv_percent_ option with the _-latency_targets_ option.
```
-ocv_delay delay
```

Adjusts the calculated early and late budget latencies so that they both vary by
at least the specified _delay_ value from the average.

When you use the _-latency_targets_ option, it is possible that OCV is not
considered. This happens if you are using ideal clocks (that is, not propagated
clocks) and you did not supply separate early and late latencies. For example, if
both the early and late latency in the design are 0, and you specify _-ocv_delay_
_0.2_, the budget latency targets are set to -0.2 and 0.2, respectively.

You must specify the _-ocv_percent_ option with the _-latency_targets_ option.




```
-host_options host_option_name
```

Specifies that the specified host option should be used for distributed
processing. The host option is created with the _set_host_options_ command.
Note that only the part of _estimate_timing_ that updates child blocks' views
supports distributed processing; therefore, this option's effect depends on the
design condition.
```
-default
```

Specifies that the default values of all the budgeting application options are
used by the tool while computing the new budget constraints. When you
use the _-default_ option, for all the application options with names of the form
_plan.budget.*_, the user-specified values are ignored.

**Description**

This command automatically assigns new budget constraints for setup delay, boundary
parasitics and drive, and/or clock latency. These parameters are controlled by using
the _-setup_delay_, _-boundary_, and _-latency_targets_ options. If you specify none of these
options, setup and boundary are assumed. See the argument descriptions above for more
information.

Note that constraints for hold delay do not depend on whether or not you run the
_compute_budget_constraints_ command. If you set the _plan.budget.write_hold_budgets_
application option to true, hold constraints is automatically calculated and output by the
_write_budgets_ command.

You can use the _compute_budget_constraints_ command to create setup delay
constraints on your budget blocks. Running this command is equivalent to running
_set_pin_budget_constraints_ directly, except that the constraints are automatically
generated. Constraints are generated to distribute slack of top-level paths to the various
budget blocks. You can use the _report_budget_ command to analyze the results.

Path delays are automatically processed and constraints are set which are the same as
those that can be manually set by the following options of the _set_pin_budget_constraints_
command:

 - -from_percent

 - -from_delay

 - -to_percent

 - -to_delay

 - -internal_percent

 - -internal_delay

This affects _set_input_delay_ and _set_output_delay_ constraints in your final budget.




Block boundaries are automatically processed and constraints are set which are the same
as those that can be manually set with the _-early_boundary_ and _-late_boundary_ options of
the _set_pin_budget_constraints_ command. This affects the _set_driving_cell_, _set_load_ and
_set_max_transition_ constraints in your final budget.

By default, _compute_budget_constraints_ processes all pins of all budget blocks. Blocks
are assigned for budgeting by the _set_budget_options -add_blocks block_name_
command. By default, all modes with an active corner are processed, unless you specify
_-modes_ .

When processing setup delays and boundary constraints, you can limit where
_compute_budget_constraints_ operates by using one or more of the _-pins_, _-input_, _-output_,
_-feedthrough_, or _-slack_ options. The _-fanin_cone_ and _-fanout_cone_ options allow
_compute_budget_constraints_ to also adjust budgets in the transitive fanin or output of
specified pins.

Use the _set_budget_options_ command to specify general options to be used
when creating timing budgets. To manually set other specific budget parameters,
use the _set_pin_budget_constraints_, _set_latency_budget_constraints_, and
_set_boundary_budget_constraints_ commands.

Use the _write_budgets_ command to generate Synopsys Design Constraint (SDC) that
can be applied to lower level blocks. The _report_budget_ command generates information
about the current budget calculation, allocation, and whether that budget is currently being
met. Use the _write_script -include budget_ command to save a Tcl script that includes your
current settings from this command.

This command returns 1 on success, 0 otherwise.

_Multiply Instantiated Blocks_

The _compute_budget_constraints_ command automatically creates equal budgets for
similar pins of multiply instantiated blocks (as directed by the _-same_as_mib_ option of
the _set_pin_budget_constraints_ command). The budget represents the best compromise
across the contexts of the multiple instances. However, if it appears that one or more
instance pins has a constraint that is impossible to meet, those constraints might be
different. You can report the pins with seemingly impossible constraints by using the
_report_budget -warning_pins_ command.

**Examples**

Automatically fill in the budget specification for any pin in any mode where no budget has
yet been specified. But before you run the following command, ensure that you do not
overwrite previously set boundary budgets.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -unspecified -setup_delay

```



Automatically fill in the budget specification for any pin in any mode where no budget has
yet been specified. Also make sure that boundary budgets are automatically created for all
pins, regardless of whether or not they have delay budgets.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -unspecified
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -boundary
```

Manually set internal delay budgets for all blocks, then use the
_compute_budget_constraints_ command to automatically fill in the unspecified feedthrough
budgets. Also make sure that boundary budgets are created for all pins.
```
prompt> set_budget_options -add_blocks { core/CPU core/MMU exif }
prompt> set_pin_budget_constraints -all -internal_percent 20
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -unspecified -feedthrough
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -boundary
```

Automatically recalculate all existing budget constraints at the input of core/CPU in the
current mode.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -input -pins core/CPU/*
```

Find any pin in "mode2" where the budget is being met by less than 0.05 nanosecond.
Assign a new budget to those pins and to pins in the fanin and fanout of those pins.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -modes mode2 -slack 0.05 \\
-fanin_cone -fanout_cone
```

Set up block clock latency targets for early in the flow. Use the current ideal clock
specifications, but enforce OCV variability.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -latency_targets actual \\
-balance true -ocv_percent 5
```

Set up block clock latency parameters for early in the flow. Use estimated latency and
OCV. Use the _-balance true_ option with the assumption that balancing will be done later in
the flow.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -latency_targets estimated \\
-balance true
```

Set up block clock latency parameters to exactly match the circuit. The _-balance false_
option assumes that the top-level clocks are already balanced.
```
prompt> compute_budget_constraints -latency_targets actual \\
-balance false
```

See the _write_budgets_ man page for more examples of the _-latency_targets_ option.




**See Also**

 - create_budget_busplan

 - report_budget

 - set_boundary_budget_constraints

 - set_budget_options

 - set_latency_budget_constraints

 - set_pin_budget_constraints

 - set_segment_budget_constraints

 - synthesize_clock_trunks

 - write_budgets

 - write_script

 - set_host_options

 - plan.budget.bbt_fixed_delay

 - plan.budget.estimate_timing_mode

 - plan.budget.time_with_margins

###### **compute_clock_latency**

Updates the network latencies of real and virtual clocks after clock tree synthesis.

**Syntax**

status _compute_clock_latency_
```
[-verbose]
```

**Data Types**

No data types

**Arguments**
```
-verbose
```

Displays additional columns in the update report to show reference clock,
latency calculation method and the number of register clock pins used to
calculate the latency.




**Description**

This command is used primarily to correct your block's timing constraints after clock
tree synthesis. Clock tree synthesis inserts clock networks, which changes the latency
on your clocks, and the apparent length of the datapaths at your block boundary. The
_compute_clock_latency_ command can adjust the clock latency on your I/O clocks so that
the datapath length is maintained and your boundary constraints are still good. See the
example below for more information.

The command calculates and updates the I/O latencies of real and virtual clock objects
for all active mode and corner combinations. To calculate and update clock latencies,
this command follows the directives set by _set_latency_adjustment_options_ command for
each mode. If no directives are given, then only the I/O latencies of real clock objects are
updated. The latencies are calculated as the median of the clock network latencies at the
clock sinks of the clock tree. For ideal clocks, a _set_clock_latency_ command is run by the
tool on the clock objects. For propagated clocks, I/O path latency is set internally on the
clock objects. The I/O path latency is used in timing the input/output ports. The command
updates latencies for all the active mode and corner combinations.

Note that _compute_clock_latency_ is run automatically by the tool as part of integrated
CTS and optimization flows. So it is important to use the _set_latency_adjustment_options_
command, even if you don't intend to call _compute_clock_latency_ explicitly.

**Multicorner-Multimode Support**

This command works on all active scenarios.

**Examples**

This example adjusts the latency on the specified I/O clocks. First, you must associate
your I/O clocks with your internal clocks by using the _set_latency_adjustment_options_
command. Then, when you run _compute_clock_latency_, the latency of the I/O clock will
be set to match your internal clock. Notice that the _write_io_constraints_ command can set
latency adjustment options with _set_latency_adjustment_options_ in the budget script.
```
prompt> set_latency_adjustment_options \\
-reference_clock my_internal_clock \\
-clocks_to_update my_io_clock
prompt> synthesize_clock_trees
prompt> compute_clock_latency
Mode:mode2      Latency(early)  Latency(late)
Clock    Updated  rise  fall  rise  fall  Corner
-----------------------------------------------------------clock    Yes   0.9336   -- 0.9336   --  c2
clock_dup  No     --   --   --   --  -clock_dup_2 Yes   1.6785   -- 1.7258   --  c2
vclk1    Yes   0.9572   -- 0.9572   --  c2
vclk2    Yes   0.9336   -- 0.9336   --  c2

```



```
Mode:mode1      Latency(early)  Latency(late)
Clock    Updated  rise  fall  rise  fall  Corner
-----------------------------------------------------------clock    Yes   0.9336   -- 0.9336   --  c1

###### **compute_dff_connections**

Traces connections in the current netlist. The results are used by the Data Flow Flylines
tool in the GUI.

**Syntax**
```
status compute_dff_connections
[-max_reg register_count ]
[-max_gate gate_count ]
[-max_fanout fanout_count ]
[-include_blocks list_of_designs ]
[-retrace_blocks list_of_designs ]
[-host_options host_option_name ]
[-work_dir working_directory ]
[-dont_include_abstracts]

```



**Data Types**
```
register_count   int
gate_count     int
fanout_count    int
list_of_designs   collection
host_option_name  string
working_directory  string
```

**Arguments**
```
-max_reg register_count
```

Specifies the maximum number of registers a path can contain and still be
stored. Paths containing more than this number of registers are not stored for
display. By default, this value is 3.
```
-max_gate gate_count
```

Specifies the maximum number of total gates a path can contain and still
be stored. Gates are considered combinational cells that are not buffers or
inverters. Paths containing more than this number of gates are not stored for
display. By default, this value is 20.
```
-max_fanout fanout_count
```

Specifies the maximum fanout permitted for any net found while tracing the path.
If a net with fanout greater than this limit is encountered, the path is not stored
for display. By default, this value is 64.
```
-include_blocks list_of_designs
```

Specifies the abstract views for which to load previously saved trace data.
The abstract view must be currently loaded or available in the library, and the
_-max_reg_, _-max_gate_, and _-max_fanout_ option values must be consistent
with the previously saved data. If no compatible trace data file exists for the
abstract view, you must also specify the _-retrace_blocks_ option. By default, the
commands loads all design views and abstract views for blocks returned by the
_get_designs_ command.
```
-retrace_blocks list_of_designs
```

Specifies a collection of abstract designs and physical blocks for which to
retrace the netlist. _list_of_designs_ is a set or subset of designs returned from
the _get_designs_ command. The specified designs are opened in design view
and traced using the current tracer settings. The trace data is saved into a
tracer data file that can be loaded by the Data Flow Flylines component in
the GUI. Any design specified for this option must also be specified for the
_-include_blocks_ option. Note: after tracing any designs in this manner, the main
design is reloaded and relinked, and all existing object collections become
invalid and must be re-created.




```
-host_options host_option_name
```

Specifies the name of the host option to use for distributed processing.
By default, this is empty and distributed processing is not used. See also
_set_host_options_ .
```
-work_dir working_directory
```

Specifies the directory in which to write the tracer files. By default, the command
writes to a directory named "work_dir".
```
-dont_include_abstracts
```

Ignores abstracts and traces only in design views.

**Description**

This command invokes the Data Flow Flylines tracer. The tracer traces through the current
netlist and stores paths that meet the specified constraints. These paths can then be
displayed using the Data Flow Flylines GUI component. Several options are available to
restrict the types of paths stored and limit the runtime required by the tracer (which might
take several minutes for a larger design).

This command uses the settings specified by the _create_dff_trace_filters_ command to stop
tracing when any of the specified filter pins or filter nets are encountered during tracing.

If the current design contains abstract blocks, they can still be included in the tracer
results. By specifying the _-include_blocks_ and _-retrace_blocks_ (if required) options, the
specified abstract view designs can be opened in design view, either in the current session
or a distributed session, depending on the current distributed processing settings. For
more information, see the man pages for _set_host_options_ and _run_block_script_ .

After saving tracer data files for the abstract designs, these sessions are closed and the
saved tracer data files can be merged into the main tracer results. This only applies to
abstract designs, and designs in design view are always automatically included in the
main tracer results.

**Examples**

The following example traces the current design using these constraints: paths with a
register depth of 2 or less, a maximum gate count of 25 or less, and a maximum fanout
of 64, which is default. The Data Flow Flylines tool can be used to view the results in the
GUI.
```
prompt> compute_dff_connections -max_reg 2 -max_gate 25
```

The following example traces the current design, but also forces a retrace of the ABS1
abstract block and includes the ABS1 and ABS2 abstract blocks in the main trace results.
```
prompt> set a1 [get_designs {ABS1 ABS2}]
{ABS1 ABS2}

```



```
prompt> set a2 [get_designs {ABS1}]
{ABS1}
prompt> compute_dff_connections -include_blocks $a1 -retrace_blocks $a2
-host_options opt1
